nested_debate.creative_editor_1: Protect the phrase as behavior, not copy decoration. 'Dekh na' is the tiny bid; the visual proof is whether the body turns.
nested_debate.creative_editor_2: The route becomes ownable when the bid is not one-way. Show both people making and answering small invitations.
nested_debate.writer_1: Cut research-language from the core slides until copy lock. The statistic should support the caption or final context, not become the carousel spine.
nested_debate.writer_2: Repair the ending away from 'good couples pay attention' and toward a felt line about ordinary things becoming shared because someone looked.

nested_debate.creative_editor_1: The universal hook is clean, but it could belong to any couple account.
nested_debate.creative_editor_2: Without the desi micro-phrase and mutual turn, it is just attention advice.
nested_debate.writer_1: Keep the verb 'looking up' as a possible copy texture later, not as the whole concept.
nested_debate.writer_2: Reject as winner unless merged into the 'dekh na' route.

nested_debate.creative_editor_1: The number is fascinating but dangerous. It invites an infographic instead of an illustrated love story.
nested_debate.creative_editor_2: Use the stat as proof-of-importance, not proof-of-love.
nested_debate.writer_1: If the first slide is a percentage, the deck starts sounding like a therapist account.
nested_debate.writer_2: Move the stat to caption or a subtle final contextual note after the scene earns it.

cross_debate_summary.what_to_protect: Small bids are tiny asks to share attention, not chores or dramatic reassurance requests.
cross_debate_summary.what_to_cut: Research infographic structure, phone-scolding, one-way patient-husband framing, and trend-copying the bird theory.
cross_debate_summary.what_to_repair: Make the bid mutual, make the visual proof physical, and make the phrase culturally specific without becoming a Hinglish gimmick.
cross_debate_summary.selector_summary: The Dekh Na Test wins because it turns a relationship-science idea into a visible A Story moment: one tiny bid, one real turn, then the turn comes back.
